Up to now, our patient has responded well to combined treatments including clonazepam, IVIG, and physical therapy. We have followed serum anti-GAD-65 titers at several time points after IVIG had worn off ( Table 1 ). While we did notice a titer rebound in serum GAD-65, TPO, ANA antibodies after 2 months pause of IVIG treatment, the patient remained clinically stable.

[...] Soon after discharge the CSF autoimmune panel revealed an abnormally elevated anti-GAD-65 antibodies at 4. 79 nmol/l, with negative amphiphysin antibodies and negative NMO/AQP4 IgG levels. Serum anti-GAD-65 antibodies were remarkably elevated at 396 nmol/l (ref < 0. 02 nmol/l) ( Table 1 ). This confirmed a diagnosis of SLS with positive anti-GAD-65 antibodies. Electromyography (EMG)/nerve conduction study was cancelled. She was subsequently started on a low dose of diazepam (2. 5 mg by mouth three times a day) for spasticity and was then admitted for intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) treatment. Diaz - epam was soon switched to clonazepam 0. 25 mg by mouth twice daily after difficulty sleeping, decreased appetite, and loose stools were re - ported as side-effects on diazepam. The patient continued to improve clinically over the next few weeks.

A lumbar puncture (LP) was pursued and the CSF routine analysis was also normal (glucose 42, protein 17, RBCs 0 and nucleated cells 2). CSF neurotransmitters ( MNG lab ) and the gene panel for neurotransmitter disorders ( Invitae ) were sent and returned later as negative. Serum amino acids (SAA), urine organic acids (UOA) and CSF amino acids were unremarkable. She had also negative Lyme titer twice, normal creatinine kinase, acylcarnitine profile, serum copper and ceruloplasmin levels.
